why: The top-8 part holds 11.8% of the delta's energy, about a = 0.12 along the switch direction, and its late-MLP readouts are deliberation/cue words; a sharply concave dose then flips most of the plain-prompt switch (a = 0.25 already gives 405/500).
Same arm on all 500: an effective dose of about 0.12 along the diffuse switch direction recovers most of the plain 224 to 463 gain on a concave curve, a little below a = 0.25's 405.
Once the switch flips the answers take RL's deliberate-then-box length, so tokens sit near the a = 0.25 plain arm (3,653), well above the plain base.
Removing the top-8 directions still leaves 88% of the delta, an unbiased dose far past saturation, so the switch stays flipped and accuracy stays at RL level (about 92%).
The bulk left after taking out the top 64 directions is still a large, diffuse fraction of the delta along every layer, and that alone saturates the switch.
24 late-MLP rank-3 terms are a tiny, localized piece of a switch the theory says is spread over every layer and matrix, so the effective dose is near zero and the plain base's ~45% stays.
RL is fully in boxed-answer mode (0% 'Answer:' lines), so the v3 grader's 'Answer:'-line fixes find almost nothing extra to credit.
RL-Zero-Mix includes math RL, so it carries the answer-mode switch and the plain prompt scores close to a cued/RL level rather than the base's 224.
Code-RL shares part of the switch (3.1 Code plain gave 390), so the 3.0 Code model's plain score sits well above the plain base but below Math RL.
The cue and the 3.0 Math RL delta flip the same saturating switch, so the cued 3.0 model lands at or a bit above the cued-base/theta level (410-457).
With the switch already selected by the cue, an RL model that has math RL scores like the cued theta arms (441-457).
Cue plus a partially shared Code-RL switch gives about the cued Code-RL 3.1 level (450), slightly lower for the weaker 3.0 run.
